title: How To Handle Overbearing Teacher Colleagues
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin offers five counterintuitive guidelines for neutralizing an overbearing, attention-dominating colleague, drawing on what he says is one of SCM's most-requested topics. The core move is to be passive and let the colleague talk as much as they want, since giving them the attention they crave tends to reduce their aggressiveness over time. He pairs this with speaking as little as possible generally, but being direct, clear, and brief when an opinion is actually needed, without hedging or over-explaining. He also stresses standing firm once a position is taken within one's own control, since caving invites more pushing around, and closes with 'be friendly' — deliberately releasing any desire for revenge or vindication, which he says paradoxically earns respect from the very colleague causing the frustration. He presents this as a long-tested, low-drama alternative to direct confrontation.
points: Let the overbearing colleague dominate discussion and speak first; giving them attention tends to reduce their aggressiveness over time.
Speak as little as possible in group settings, offering opinions only when directly asked or when a group decision requires it.
When you do state an opinion, be direct and brief — don't hedge, over-explain, or get pulled into an argument.
Once you've taken a position within your own control, don't waver; caving invites the colleague to push harder.
Let go of any desire for revenge or vindication — this paradoxically earns the colleague's respect over time.
quotes: They dominate every meeting. They brag about and must share the way they do things and hardly listen to anyone else.

You must let go of any desire to be in charge and allow them to lead discussions and group meetings. By giving them what they want—to be heard and taken seriously—they tend to relax and temper their aggressiveness.
It’s important that you don’t bring up topics that get them off track. The best way to do this is to just be quiet. Speak as little as possible.
This is especially important: When it’s time to offer your opinion, do so directly, clearly, and with as few words as possible. Do not hem and haw or beat around the bush.

Once you’ve decided on a path that is in your control, don’t waver for anything in the world. Do not give in. As soon as you do, you’ll lose their respect and they’ll try to push you around even more.
The old adage to keep your friends close and your enemies closer is a truism based on this wisdom.
